Task Name: Start PCB planning for sensors, ESP32, buttons, display, and power
Task Content:
PCB Planning — Decisions & Notes

Power Section

Charging IC: TP4056 (or MCP73831 if slightly better quality is wanted)
No power-path — battery cycles during USB use
Acceptable trade-off for capstone timeline: only ~30–50 equivalent full cycles over the project life
BQ24074 (with power-path) was considered but rejected for now: ~$3 IC cost is fine, but adds layout complexity and respin risk on the main board
Revisit BQ24074 only if a respin is happening anyway and we want the upgrade
Main 3.3V regulator: Buck converter — see "Research voltage regulators for the PCB" task for details
5V rail: Boost converter from LiPo (e.g. MT3608, TPS61023)
Needed for the LCD (most decently-sized TFT options need 5V or are 5V-tolerant) and potentially for an addressable LED array
USB-C already provides 5V when plugged in — boost only needed when on battery
Cheap (~$0.50 IC) and standard
No 12V rail planned — nothing in current BOM requires it
Adding 12V would require either a boost from LiPo (high ratio, noisy, inefficient) or switching to a 2S/3S LiPo pack (expensive, complex charging)
Revisit only if a specific stretch-goal component is identified that needs 12V
Hard SPST power switch wired directly to LiPo output (per D&C doc)
USB-C connector wired for 5V input only (no PD negotiation needed)

Rail Summary

[table-embed:1:1 Rail | 1:2 Source | 1:3 Loads | 2:1 VBAT (3.0–4.2V) | 2:2 LiPo directly | 2:3 Buck input, boost input | 3:1 3.3V | 3:2 Buck from VBAT | 3:3 ESP32, phototransistors, logic | 4:1 5V | 4:2 Boost from VBAT (or USB-C direct when plugged in) | 4:3 LCD, optional LED array |]
ESP32 Module

Primary choice: ESP32-WROOM-32E
Cheap (~$3), well-documented, plenty of GPIO for the sensor mux strategy
Keep ESP32-S3 viable as a backup in case scope expands
S3 has native USB (no separate UART-to-USB chip needed), more RAM, useful if ML/heavier processing is added
Note: S3 footprint is NOT pin-compatible with WROOM-32E, but WROOM-32U IS (same footprint, different antenna)
Action item for layout: keep regulator, programming header, boot/EN button circuitry generic enough that swapping module families is not catastrophic

Sensor Mux Strategy (still TBD)

400 phototransistors → definitely multiplexing
Likely candidates: 74HC4067 (16-ch analog mux) or ADG732 (32-ch)
Need to decide channel count per mux and total mux count → drives GPIO budget for select lines
Plan column/row scanning vs full-array mux tree

Display (leaning graphical TFT, not character LCD)

Group wants "decently sized" display showing accuracy info → character LCD insufficient (text only)
Realistic candidates:
2.4–2.8" SPI TFT (ILI9341) — ~$8–15, 320×240
3.5–4" SPI TFT (ILI9488) — ~$15–25, 480×320, probably best size match for the 6" control area
Nextion HMI 3.5–5" — ~$25–50, has own MCU, easier UI design, UART interface
Most TFTs run on 3.3V or 5V — confirms need for 5V rail
Interface: SPI most common; Nextion uses UART
Action: pick specific module before finalizing connector footprint and pinout

LED Hit-Indicator Array (open question — see separate research task)

Feasibility of 400-LED-per-sensor array still being evaluated
TFT display can already show shot placement → array may be redundant
If pursued: addressable (WS2812) is more practical than discrete (shift registers + 400 traces)
See research task for full breakdown

Buttons / Input

4–6 push buttons per D&C doc
External 10k pull-ups on PCB (more reliable than internal ESP32 pull-ups)
Software debouncing — no RC filters needed at this count
Direct GPIO connections, no I/O expander needed

Layout Priorities

Keep analog (phototransistor) and digital (ESP32, LCD) ground domains separated, single-point star ground
Bulk cap close to ESP32 power pin
If buck-only design causes noise: leave footprint for downstream LDO on analog rail
Programming header (UART + boot + EN + GND + 3V3) accessible from removable back panel per enclosure design
Boost converter and buck converter should be physically separated from analog sensor traces

Open Items

Finalize buck IC selection
Finalize boost IC selection for 5V rail
Decide analog mux part + channel architecture
Confirm LCD module + interface (driven by size, cost, library support)
Resolve LED array feasibility (see separate research task)
Estimate total active current draw → size battery accordingly
Decide whether to leave footprint for optional LDO on analog rail

Task Name: Research voltage regulators for the PCB
Task Content:
Voltage Regulator Research — Decisions & Notes

Current Direction

Main 3.3V rail: Buck converter (e.g. TPS62130, MP2307, RT8059)

Chosen for battery life — 85–95% efficient vs. LDO burning the voltage delta as heat
Trade-off: switching noise could affect analog phototransistor readings
Fallback plan: If noise becomes a problem during prototyping, add a small downstream LDO (MCP1700 / TLV75533) specifically for the phototransistor reference voltage

Why not LDO as the primary?

AMS1117-3.3 dropout is ~1.1V — would stop regulating around 3.4V battery and lose usable LiPo capacity
Lower-dropout LDOs (MCP1700, TLV75533) are options if buck noise turns out to be unworkable
Heat dissipation at 4.2V → 3.3V @ 500mA (~450mW) is manageable but wasteful for a battery-powered device

Open items

Pick specific buck IC (compare TPS62130 vs MP2307 vs RT8059 on cost / availability / footprint)
Calculate expected peak current draw (ESP32 TX bursts + active sensor mux channels + LCD backlight)
Decide on inductor + output cap values once IC is picked
Plan analog rail filtering (ferrite bead + bulk cap) in case noise mitigation is needed
If LDO backup is added, route phototransistor Vcc separately from digital rail

Reference: ESP32 power needs

Idle: ~20–80 mA
Wi-Fi / BLE TX peaks: up to ~500 mA short bursts
Needs decent bulk cap at the module power pin regardless of regulator choice

Task Name: Evaluate LED hit-indicator array: addressable vs discrete vs drop
Task Content:
LED Hit-Indicator Array — Feasibility Research

Context

The D&C doc describes an LED array that lights up at the position of detected laser hits, with one LED per sensor (up to 400 LEDs). Since the project will likely also include a graphical TFT display showing shot placement, the per-sensor LED array becomes a question of wow factor vs. practical necessity rather than a core requirement.

This task is to evaluate the three realistic paths and bring a recommendation back to the group.

Option 1: Drop the per-sensor LED array entirely

Use the TFT display alone for shot visualization (target rendered with shot dots overlaid)
Keep ~5–10 discrete LEDs for system status (power, mode indicator, hit/miss flash, calibration)
Savings: ~$50–80 in parts, significant PCB complexity, no LED parasitic drain
Trade-off: Less "wow factor" during demo; visualization is screen-only
Arguably the TFT shows shot data better than a coarse LED grid mapped to sensor positions

Option 2: Smaller addressable accent ring

~16–32 WS2812 LEDs around the target ring (not per-sensor)
Used for general feedback: zone hit colors, calibration animation, score indication
Cost: ~$5–10 in parts
Power: minimal parasitic drain (~16–32 mA idle)
PCB: single data line, trivial routing
Good middle ground — adds visual feedback without per-sensor complexity

Option 3: Full 400-LED per-sensor grid (the D&C-spec version)

Addressable (WS2812) is the only sane choice — discrete + 50 shift registers + 400 traces is a PCB nightmare for the same final cost
Cost: ~$50–80 in parts (strip-form addressable LEDs at ~$0.10–0.20 per LED)
Power gotchas:
Idle parasitic drain: ~400 mA just from the controller chips in each LED, even with all LEDs off
Active draw is fine — only a few LEDs lit at a time (~100–300 mA peak)
Mitigation: add a load switch (e.g. P-channel MOSFET + GPIO control) to cut the LED rail when array isn't actively displaying
5V rail required (already planned)
PCB complexity: single data line still, but 400 LED footprints take up real estate next to the 400 phototransistor footprints — alignment and physical layout becomes a serious challenge

Comparison Table

[table-embed:8:1 | 8:2 | 8:3 | 8:4 | 1:1 Factor| 1:2 Drop (Option 1)| 1:3 Accent Ring (Option 2)| 1:4 Full Grid (Option 3)| 2:1 Parts cost| 2:2 ~$2–5| 2:3 ~$5–10| 2:4 ~$50–80| 3:1 PCB complexity| 3:2 Trivial| 3:3 Trivial| 3:4 High (400 footprints + alignment)| 4:1 Software complexity| 4:2 Low| 4:3 Low| 4:4 Low (FastLED handles it)| 5:1 Idle power| 5:2 ~0| 5:3 ~16–32 mA| 5:4 ~400 mA (without load switch)| 6:1 Demo wow factor| 6:2 Low| 6:3 Medium| 6:4 High| 7:1 Redundant with TFT?| 7:2 N/A| 7:3 No — different role| 7:4 Somewhat|]
Discrete vs Addressable (for reference)

If discrete LEDs were used instead:

74HC595 shift registers, 8 LEDs per chip → 50 chips for 400 LEDs
~$30 total parts cost (cheaper than addressable!)
BUT: 400 individual LED traces, single color only, PWM brightness is annoying
Verdict: discrete only makes sense for a small fixed number of status LEDs, not for any array larger than ~16

Recommendation (for group discussion)

Lean toward Option 1 or 2 for the capstone:

TFT already shows shot placement → primary visualization is covered
Option 2 adds polish without committing to the per-sensor grid
Option 3 is a real stretch goal — feasible but eats budget, PCB area, and adds power complexity

If the group strongly wants Option 3 for the demo, plan the load switch from day one to handle the parasitic drain.

Action Items

Bring this comparison to the group for a feasibility / scope discussion
Decision blocks: PCB layout finalization, LED parts ordering, 5V boost converter sizing
If Option 3: research load-switch options (e.g. SiP32431, AP2127, simple P-MOSFET high-side switch)
Confirm TFT choice in parallel — if Nextion route is chosen, that may reduce need for hardware LED feedback further
